messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya is a 25-year-old South Asian counselor who works at a community mental health center. Six months ago, she was walking home from an evening shift when police officers stopped her, accusing her of matching a suspect description. They shoved her to the ground, pressed a knee into her back, and held her face against the soil. She was released without charges, but the smell of earth, the weight of the officer’s body, and the sound of his voice stayed with her.

In the weeks after, Priya found that riding the bus—her only route to work—became unbearable. The moment she stepped on, the faint smell of outdoor dirt would trigger a full sensory reliving: she would feel the grit against her cheek, hear the shouted commands, and her body would stiffen into the same pinned position. And each time the memory surfaced, the danger felt immediate — as if the officers had just arrived and were about to give a command she would not be able to follow. This often happened before she had time to think; her body reacted to danger before her mind caught up. To cope, she started covering her face with her hands whenever she saw a police officer—even in a passing car—certain they could see the contamination she felt on her skin. That certainty made every step she took feel like moving through hostile territory — the threat was already inside her before she ever saw a uniform. She began checking mirrors constantly, scanning for anyone following her.

Priya came to believe that people are not what they seem, that even the most familiar face could hide threat. She studied passengers’ body language, looking for signs of aggression. This hypervigilance, in turn, made the memory return more frequently: a sudden frown on a stranger’s face would drag her back to the officer’s expression as he leaned over her. Living in that constant state of alarm, she had come to accept that the world was as unsafe as she had first feared — and that she was too weak to withstand it. After the memory had broken through so vividly, she found she could no longer walk past a parked patrol car without her stomach dropping — the image had sharpened every edge of her world. She felt dirty, as if the event had permanently stained her, and this sense of contamination made her avoid friends she used to socialize with—she was certain they could see it, too, or that she no longer belonged in their world. Because she saw herself as marked, she started noticing police officers in places she had never registered them before — outside the grocery store, waiting at the crosswalk, parked in the lot behind the clinic. The isolation deepened her feeling of having lost her connection to community and culture, and that loss made every police encounter feel more threatening, more personal.

At night, she had difficulty falling asleep because she needed to stay alert; any creak or outside sound could trigger a flashback, and she would relive the moment with a strange numbness, as if it had happened to someone else, only to be followed seconds later by her body reenacting the position. That high alert meant that ordinary sensations — a car door closing, the whir of a bus engine, a shout from across the street — all became warnings she could not dismiss. But on nights when the alertness was at its peak, the memory surfaced on its own — not triggered by a sound, but pulled up by the body's readiness for danger. The memory itself drove her maladaptive strategies: after a full reliving on the bus, she would cover her face and avoid social eye contact, which then reinforced her belief that she was contaminated. The more she covered and avoided, the more isolated she became, and the more isolated she felt, the more she noticed police officers on every street corner.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was an incident on the bus last week. A passenger wearing a uniform triggered a severe reenactment—she froze, covered her face, and could not get off for two stops. Her supervisor at the counseling center saw her arrive shaken and urged her to talk to someone. Priya is afraid that she is losing her ability to do her job, where she once helped others process trauma. She hopes to stop feeling like a stranger in her own body and to reclaim the sense of belonging she has lost.
